lesson.title: The Rise of the American City
lesson.summary: Fed by the new immigration wave and by the rail network that connected farms to factories, American cities grew at an explosive pace in the late nineteenth century, reshaping where and how most Americans lived.
lesson.body:
The same forces driving the new immigration wave, industrial jobs concentrated in cities and a rail network that could move people quickly across the country, also pulled millions of native born rural Americans off the farm and into urban centers. Many were farmers squeezed out by mechanization and falling crop prices; others were workers simply chasing the steady wages that city factories offered. Immigrants and rural migrants together crowded into the same expanding urban neighborhoods.

The scale of urban growth in this period was extraordinary. Chicago, in particular, rebuilt itself at astonishing speed after the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed much of the city, emerging within a generation as one of the country's great industrial metropolises. By the 1920 census, for the first time in American history, more Americans lived in cities than in the countryside.

New technology made this density possible. Electric streetcars let cities expand outward along fixed routes, and steel frame construction let buildings rise higher than ever before. Chicago's Home Insurance Building, completed in 1885 and designed by the architect William Le Baron Jenney, is often cited as one of the first true skyscrapers, a building type that would soon define the American city skyline.

This rapid, largely unplanned growth also created serious problems: severe housing shortages, inadequate sanitation and clean water, overcrowded streets, air and water pollution, and rising crime, all concentrated most heavily in poor and immigrant neighborhoods living in sharp contrast to the city's wealthier districts. Two very different responses to this disorder would follow: crowded tenement housing built to squeeze as many residents as possible into limited space, and informal political machines that stepped in to manage, and often exploit, a city government too weak to keep up on its own.
